catalog_quote: [Kilgour & Hendrickson 1992, 1.4 p.113] Stress is contrastive in Bantoanon words. A stress group is the phonological unit within which syllables are distributed. The nucleus of each stress group is the primary stressed syllable ['v] which may be optionally followed by one unstressed syllable. ... If the stress group nucleus is an open syllable, the vowel is slightly lengthened. Stress groups consisting of from one to four syllables have been observed in the language. Primary stress ['] favours the penultimate or ultimate syllable of the stress group. Secondary stress ["] may optionally occur on the second syllable preceding the syllable with primary stress. ... In stressed closed syllables the vowel appears louder, rather than lengthened, though sometimes there may be a slight lengthening on stressed, word final closed syllables. ... [3.3 p.134] There is contrastive stress in Bantoanon.…

The accent position does vary across headwords (final abá / ka-aduhán, penult abága / bandílyo / ka-ámpin, antepenult ábaka), so a per-word contrastive accent is the only reading the dictionary supports; it states no plac…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a Bantoanon record with an empty rule; the dictionary supplies the type (per-word, contrastive accent in penult, final or antepenult position) but no rule sentence. Its 'Entries explained' page is the only prose about accent; the Alphabet, Introduction, Download ('Coming later..') and Language pages say nothing about stress, and no PDF of the dictionary is offered.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary gives no placement rule; it marks the accent on every headword individually (the site calls the acute accents 'tone markings'), and the marked position varies from word to word: final (abá, ka-aduhán), penult (abadáwan, abága, bandílyo, ka-ámpin) and antepenult (ábaka). Stress is therefore treated as a lexical property of each word, which is what a per-entry marking convention implies.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated; one accent per headword (the grave in abagamútà marks a final glottal stop, not a second stress).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Nothing on tone; the 'tone markings' wording is the Webonary template's label for the accent marks.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary's Introduction lists the dialects Banton, Calatravanhon, Odionganon, Sibalenhon (Sibale) and Simaranhon and does not say which variety the headword accents represent (an entry note refers to Banton Island); the 1984 manuscript is titled simply 'Bantoanon'. Both sources treat the language as one unit, so no dialect-specific claim is made.

new_statements.quote: There is contrastive stress in Bantoanon. It is manifested as length on the vowel nucleus of open syllables, but in closed syllables the prominence is usually voice emphasis or loudness. In word-final open syllables the vowel has a breathy quality similar to length but phonologically sounding like a vowel followed by [h]. [...] A pitch difference is not consistent. Sometimes the whole syllable is also lengthened or there is a slowing of the speed so that the syllables appear so similar that it is hard to distinguish which one is stressed. This difficulty is more noticeable with words of two closed syllables. The contrasting stress is illustrated in the following words. /kítaq/ [kíː.tʌʔ] 'see' /kitá/ [ki.táh] 'we (inclusive)' /qúbus/ [ˈúː.bos] 'used up' /qubús/ [ˈu.bós] 'down below' /sípit/ [síː.pɪt] 'clothes pin' /sipít/ [si.pít] 'hair clips'

new_statements.relation_note: Same compiler as the dictionary; gives the explicit statement that stress is contrastive and the minimal pairs, filling the catalog's empty rule field. Consistent with the dictionary's per-headword accent marks.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (contrastive): disyllables can be stressed on either the penult or the final syllable, with minimal pairs (kítaq 'see' vs kitá 'we incl.', qúbus 'used up' vs qubús 'down below', sípit 'clothes pin' vs sipít 'hair clips'). Its main cue is vowel length in open syllables, loudness in closed syllables, and a breathy [h] offglide on stressed word-final open vowels; pitch is not a consistent cue.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; the authors note stress is hard to hear in words of two closed syllables, and that the final [h] of stressed open final syllables surfaces as /h/ under affixation.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary's Introduction lists the dialects Banton, Calatravanhon, Odionganon, Sibalenhon (Sibale) and Simaranhon and does not say which variety the headword accents represent (an entry note refers to Banton Island); the 1984 manuscript is titled simply 'Bantoanon'. Both sources treat the language as one unit, so no dialect-specific claim is made.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held K&H 1992 PDF at the stated pages (p.113 text layer; p.134 page image with the four minimal pairs). The source is the language's only dedicated phonological description, by long-term SIL fieldworkers, and Glottolog/OLAC show nothing better (no reference grammar, no instrumental study). The 1984 manuscript version, downloaded now from the SIL archive via the Internet Archive, states the same contrastive-stress analysis with the same minimal pairs, and Zorc 1977 agrees comparatively. lexical / right-edge two-syllable window / word domain stands; the third reader's decision to drop the Zorc closed-penult sub-rule is supported by K&H's own transcriptions (p.121 vs p.133). Only a low-priority dictionary check remains on the list of works to obtain.
